name: Table Mountain
label: Table Mountain
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Signal Hill' (2 web pages); placed at our map tiles: 'Signal Hill Drive' (roads).
pin_note: Position set at the correction gate (pin check 2026-11-17: moved onto the OSM object with the sight's Wikidata ID).
notes: The flat-topped mountain that defines the Cape Town skyline.

text.description: Table Mountain is the flat-topped mountain that rises behind Cape Town, and it is a prominent landmark overlooking the city. The level plateau is roughly three kilometres from side to side, edged by steep cliffs, with Devil's Peak to the east and Lion's Head to the west. The top stands about 1,000 metres above the streets below, so even from a distance it fills a good part of the frame. It also holds around 2,285 plant species, about 80% of them fynbos, which is why the low bushes near your feet make a natural foreground. From Signal Hill you see the mountain side-on, so the cliffs and the long flat edge show up clearly, with Lion's Head alongside. The mountain is often covered by a layer of cloud known as the 'table cloth', which can hide the plateau or spill over it, so look at the forecast and be ready to wait a little. Keep the horizon level and leave a strip of fynbos along the bottom of the picture to give a sense of scale. If you want a different view, Kloof Corner frames the mountain against the sky and city, but it is a steep walk. Bloubergstrand shows the whole front of the mountain across the bay, about 20 minutes' drive north of the city.
text.geographic_location: Table Mountain rises directly above Cape Town's City Bowl, with Lion's Head to its west and Devil's Peak to its east.
text.directions_text: There are no Underground, train or tram stops for this spot, so start from the City Bowl and head north-west up towards Signal Hill. Aim for the quieter small car park near the top rather than the main upper car park, then follow the hiking path from it. Parking is limited near sunset, so arrive early. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start on the default lens (1x) to see the whole scene. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) if you want fynbos close to the lens and Lion's Head in the same frame. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out the cliffs and the straight edge of the plateau.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Signal Hill (the quieter small car park near the top and the hiking path leading from it, away from the main upper car park). Table Mountain seen from the side, with its cliffs and flat plateau, alongside Lion's Head, with fynbos in the foreground.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and put the plateau's top edge on one of the horizontal lines so it stays straight. Keep roughly the bottom third for the fynbos and the mountain in the upper two thirds. A panorama works if you sweep slowly from Lion's Head across to the plateau. Hold the phone steady and keep it level while it sweeps.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the cliffs to focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the sky is bright so the cloud keeps its detail. If cloud is moving over the top, take a Live Photo or a few quick shots and choose the best one.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Sunrise is recommended for this view, and the small car park is quieter than the main one. If you go for sunset, arrive early because parking fills up.

text.access_note: Signal Hill is an open park viewpoint, but parking is limited near sunset, and for anything within Table Mountain National Park, check the official site before you go.

photo.artist: Danie van der Merwe from Cape Town, South Africa

name: Clifton
label: Clifton Beaches
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'The Rock' (1 web pages); placed at our map tiles: 'Sunset Rock' (pois).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/2034682: large area 'Clifton' (2009 m across): previous pin kept, it lies inside.
notes: Four sheltered beaches among granite boulders.

text.description:
Clifton is a string of four small beaches on the Atlantic side of Cape Town, split from one another by big rounded granite boulders. The beaches are numbered 1st to 4th from north to south, and the sand is almost pure white. That gives you a clean pale curve of sand, dark boulders and blue water in the same frame, which is why it works so well on a phone. Houses climb the slope behind, and Lion's Head rises above them.

The beaches are well sheltered from the strong south-easter, which is part of their popularity. The sand moves with the seasons. In winter it is stripped away and the boulders stand out more. By late summer the beaches are at their widest. Fourth Beach is the busiest and most glamorous of the four, and it has Blue Flag status.

For this photo, go to the point near The Rock, at the end of Ocean View Drive. From this higher angle you look down onto the beaches and the boulders between them. It is a quieter view than the beach itself. Stay well back from the edge of the boulders. For a second angle, walk down to Clifton 4th Beach for the white sand and turquoise shallows, with the Twelve Apostles ridge and Lion's Head behind. Kloof Road is another option, with a high view over the coves towards Camps Bay and Table Mountain. It is a busy winding road, so keep to the pavement or a safe verge.
text.geographic_location: Clifton is a seaside suburb on Cape Town's Atlantic Seaboard, between Bantry Bay and Camps Bay, with Lion's Head mountain behind it. The viewpoint is at the end of Ocean View Drive, on the high ground above the beaches.
text.directions_text: There are no Underground, train or tram stops for this spot, so guides recommend driving to the end of Ocean View Drive and parking there. Then walk from the parking spots to the point near The Rock. Driving is the sensible way to arrive, because the viewpoint is on a road end rather than beside a stop. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) to take in the beaches and boulders together. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if you want more of the coast and sky. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out one beach or the pattern of boulders.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on The Rock (Ocean View Drive, at the end of the road; walk from the parking spots to the point near The Rock). An elevated view looking south down onto the Clifton beaches and the boulders between them. Stay on the walking path from the parking spots and do not climb onto the boulders or out to their edge.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Switch on gridlines and put the line of the beaches along a lower third, with the sea and sky above. Use the boulders in the foreground to lead the eye down the coast. For a different angle, try Clifton 4th Beach, where Lion's Head and the Twelve Apostles sit behind the sand. Kloof Road gives a high view towards Camps Bay and Table Mountain.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the sand to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the white sand does not wash out. A short panorama along the coast also works well if you hold the phone steady.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Choose a clear day, and check the weather before you set off, because haze and cloud flatten the colours of the sea.

text.access_note: The point near The Rock is reached by a short walk from the parking spots at the end of Ocean View Drive; check the official site and local signs before you go for any parking or access restrictions.

name: V&A Waterfront
label: V&A Waterfront
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Yellow Frame' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Table Mountain Yellow Frame (District Six)' (node/11391420945): point.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/422454667: large area 'V&A Waterfront' (1272 m across): previous pin kept, it lies inside.
notes: Working harbour with shops, restaurants and mountain views.

text.description:
The V&A Waterfront is a working harbour area on Table Bay, with shops, restaurants, hotels and marina basins, and Table Mountain rising behind it. It stands on the oldest working harbour in the Southern Hemisphere. The story goes back to 1654, when Jan van Riebeeck built a small jetty here to supply passing ships. The two harbour basins were built between 1860 and 1920, and several buildings from that era are still standing.

For a phone photo, the easiest classic shot is at the large yellow picture frame on the harbour side, near the Den Anker restaurant. Table Mountain sits neatly inside the frame, so the picture is composed for you, and the harbour and city skyline are behind you. It works well for a photo of the mountain on its own, or of a friend standing in the frame.

If you have time for a second picture, Nobel Square puts four bronze statues in front of the mountain. The Clock Tower, built in 1882 and now leaning very slightly, gives a quieter, more architectural view with reflections on the water. Expect other visitors to be taking the same photo, so be patient and take a few frames while people move through.
text.geographic_location: The V&A Waterfront is a district of Cape Town on the Table Bay harbour edge, just north of the city centre and with Table Mountain as its backdrop. The Yellow Frame is on the harbour side, near the Den Anker restaurant.
text.directions_text: No Underground, train or tram stop is listed for this spot, so start from the city centre of Cape Town and head north towards the harbour. Once you are in the Waterfront, look for the harbour side and the Den Anker restaurant, and the Yellow Frame is close by. Positions of the frame can shift slightly, so check on arrival. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) so the mountain fills the frame naturally. Try the ultra-wide (0.5x) if you want more of the frame and sky, and the telephoto (2x or more, depending on your phone) to bring the mountain closer.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject (on the harbour side, near the Den Anker restaurant; stand inside the frame and face Table Mountain). Table Mountain framed by the large yellow picture frame, with the harbour and city skyline behind the photographer.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and line the mountain up with the centre of the frame, keeping the horizon level. Hold the phone steady and square on, and keep the frame edges even on both sides. For a different picture, Nobel Square gives the bronze statues with the mountain behind, and the Clock Tower is a quieter option.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the mountain to set focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the sky looks washed out. Use portrait mode if you are photographing a person in the frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Choose a clear day when Table Mountain is not covered by cloud. Go early if you want fewer people in the frame.

text.access_note: The Waterfront is a busy public area, but rules on photography can apply, so check the official site before you go.

name: Table Mountain Aerial Cableway
label: Table Mountain Cable
camera_source: No separate stand-here point: photographed at the spot itself (indoors, from its top, or right in front of it); drawn as the split pin.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/913810869: the middle of the OpenStreetMap line 'Table Mountain Cableway' (999 m long).
notes: Rotating cable car with sweeping views of the city and bay.

text.description: The Table Mountain Aerial Cableway is the cable car that carries visitors to the top of Table Mountain in about five minutes. It is one of Cape Town's most popular attractions, with roughly a million people riding it each year. It opened on 4 October 1929 and has been upgraded three times since. The current 'Rotair' cars date from 1997. Each holds 65 passengers, and the floor turns through 360 degrees during the trip, so everyone gets a turn at the view without moving. That makes it unusually good for phone photos: the scene keeps changing around you as you rise. The upper station sits at the western end of the plateau, 1,067 metres up. From there the views run north over Cape Town, Table Bay and Robben Island, and west and south along the Atlantic coast. The phone icon on the map is halfway along the cableway's route, so this is a ride-time photo. Get a spot near a window early, hold your phone close to the glass and let the floor rotate. Take a few frames each time the view changes: the city, the sea, then the rock face. At the top, the views are there for the taking. Check the official site before you go, as the cableway can be affected by weather and operating changes.
text.geographic_location: On Table Mountain in Cape Town, South Africa. The route runs up to the upper station at the western end of the plateau, which looks north over the city and Table Bay.
text.directions_text: No train or tram stops are listed for this spot, so travel from central Cape Town to the lower cableway station. The cableway then carries you up the mountain to the upper station at the western end of the plateau. Check the official operator's site before you go for current operating details. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) inside the cabin to fit in the view, other passengers and the mountain. Use the default lens (1x) for cleaner shots of a single scene through the glass. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for details such as Robben Island or the city blocks below.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. The subject is the cableway and the scene around it, so stand by a window and shoot outwards, or back at the car and the cable ahead.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and keep the horizon level as the floor turns. Take a wide shot first, then move in on one feature, such as the coastline, the city or the rock face. Press your phone gently against the glass, or hold it very close, to cut down reflections. Avoid covering the lens with your hand or strap.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the scenery outside, not the glass, to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly so the sky keeps its colour. Try a Live Photo or short video to catch the rotating view. Panorama mode is better kept for the top, as the moving floor will blur it.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light and slightly fewer people. Choose a clear day, because cloud can hide the view.

text.access_note: Check the official operator's site before you go for current operating details.
claims_not_in_sources: Holding a phone close to the glass reduces reflections in cabin photos.
Panorama mode tends to blur when the floor is rotating.
Morning or late afternoon often gives softer light and fewer crowds.
Cloud can hide the view from the cableway and the summit.
The cableway's operation can be affected by weather.

name: Camps Bay
label: Camps Bay Beach
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Camps Bay Viewpoint' (2 web pages); placed at our map tiles: 'POD Camps Bay' (pois); moved 10 m off buildings.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/2034681: large area 'Camps Bay' (3650 m across): previous pin kept, it lies inside.
notes: White-sand beach backed by the Twelve Apostles mountains.

text.description:
Camps Bay is a small bay on the Atlantic side of the Cape Peninsula, with a long curve of white sand and the jagged Twelve Apostles ridge rising straight behind it. That backdrop is why it photographs so well. You get sea, sand, mountain and sky in one frame, and on clear days Lion's Head shows up too. Camps Bay Beach is the largest white sand beach in the area and has been a Blue Flag beach since 2008. Across the road is the main run of hotels, restaurants and shops, which adds colour and life to a wide shot.

The area has been a day-out spot for a long time. Victoria Road was finished in 1887, and in 1901 a tramway brought visitors out for the day, along with tidal pools and a pavilion for concerts.

For the best picture, start at Camps Bay Viewpoint, a free roadside terrace that is open all the time. It sits higher than the sand, so you can look over the whole beach to the mountains. If you want a lower, closer view, walk down to the beach itself, or to the tidal pool, where still water can mirror the sky. Don't climb onto the rocks for a shot. Parking near the viewpoint can be hard at busy times, so allow a little extra time.
text.geographic_location: Camps Bay is a coastal suburb on Cape Town's Atlantic Seaboard, on the west side of the Cape Peninsula below the Twelve Apostles. Victoria Road runs along the shore, linking it to Clifton and Sea Point to the north.
text.directions_text: MyCiTi routes 106 and 107 stop along Victoria Road, so check the current timetable. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to take in the whole bay, beach and mountains. Then switch to the default lens (1x) for a more natural view. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out the ridge of the Twelve Apostles or Lion's Head on a clear day.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Camps Bay Viewpoint. A raised panorama over the bay, the beach, the Twelve Apostles and, on clear days, Lion's Head.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and place the horizon on the upper or lower line rather than in the middle. Keep a strip of beach at the bottom and the mountain ridge along the top. If you want a lower, closer view, Camps Bay Beach gives white sand and sea in the foreground. Camps Bay Tidal Pool can give a calm reflection of the sky with the mountains behind.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the mountains to set focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the sky keeps its colour and the sand does not turn white. Try a panorama along the curve of the bay, moving slowly and keeping the phone level.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Sunrise or golden hour, as visitors are advised. Check on arrival which end of the beach gives the better view, as opinions differ.

text.access_note: The viewpoint is a free, open roadside overlook and the beach is a public beach, but check the official site before you go in case anything has changed.

name: Bo-Kaap
label: Bo-Kaap
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Wale Street and Chiappini Street intersection' (2 web pages); placed at crossing of Wale Street and Chiappini Street (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/2034623: large area 'Bo-Kaap' (1541 m across): previous pin kept, it lies inside.
notes: Hillside streets of brightly painted houses.

text.description:
Bo-Kaap is the steep, cobbled neighbourhood of brightly painted houses on the slopes of Signal Hill, just above Cape Town's city centre. It is the historic heart of Cape Malay culture in the city, and it photographs well because of the colour. Pink, red, blue, green and purple facades sit side by side, and the streets run uphill so the rows seem to step up the slope. On a clear day Table Mountain fills the far end of the view.

It is also one of the oldest parts of Cape Town. It is the oldest surviving residential neighbourhood in the city, and it has the largest concentration of pre-1850 buildings in South Africa. In 2019, 19 sites here were declared National Heritage sites. The bright paint is often put down to the new owners' sense of freedom after emancipation, though the colourful look seems to date mainly from the late 20th century.

The best-known frame is at the corner of Wale Street and Chiappini Street, where two rows of differently coloured houses meet. Expect other visitors there, so wait for a gap. For a calmer picture, try Helliger Lane, a narrow lane of pastel houses, but check it still looks as described. People live here, so keep a respectful distance from front doors and steps.
text.geographic_location: Bo-Kaap sits on the lower slopes of Signal Hill, immediately above the Cape Town city centre (the City Bowl).
text.directions_text: There are no nearby rail or tram stops for this spot. Start from the Cape Town city centre and walk up Wale Street to the corner with Chiappini Street. Streets here are steep and cobbled, so wear flat, grippy shoes. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the corner itself. Try telephoto at 2x or 3x if your phone has it, which also helps you pick out one row of houses from the crowd. Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) only in narrow lanes, and keep the phone level so the houses don't lean.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand at the corner of Wale Street and Chiappini Street (diagonal corner of the intersection, looking down the hill). Two colourful facade rows meeting at the corner, with the downhill view of Wale Street and Table Mountain at the far end when the sky is clear.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Switch on the gridlines and place the corner where two grid lines cross, with the downhill street leading the eye towards the mountain. Wait a moment for people to move out of the frame. For a quieter alternative, walk to Wale Street itself for the row of houses stepping up the slope, or to Helliger Lane for pastel houses along a narrow lane.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on a brightly painted wall to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the colours stay rich and the sky does not wash out. If Table Mountain looks faint, tap on the sky rather than the houses.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning, in the first two hours after sunrise. Tour groups tend to build up after about 8 am, so you will have more space before then.

text.access_note: Bo-Kaap is a residential neighbourhood, so please don't sit or lean on people's steps, don't photograph residents without asking, and don't approach front doors; for the Bo-Kaap Museum or any mosque, check the official site before you go.

name: District Six Museum
label: District Six Museum
camera_source: No separate stand-here point: photographed at the spot itself (indoors, from its top, or right in front of it); drawn as the split pin.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/250299433: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'District Six Museum' (46 m across).
notes: Museum remembering the forced removals of District Six.

text.description: The District Six Museum sits in an old Methodist church in the former inner-city district of District Six, in Cape Town. It is a museum and a memorial in one, so the photos you take here tend to be about the building and its setting rather than a grand view. The church exterior is the easiest subject from the street. The foundation behind it was set up in 1989 and the museum opened in 1994, as a memorial to the forced removal of about 60,000 people of various races from District Six during apartheid in the 1970s. Inside, the floor is covered by a large map of the district, with handwritten notes from former residents showing where their homes stood. There are also old street signs and displays about family life and the demolition. For a phone photo, stand at the phone icon on the map and frame the whole front of the building, keeping the sides level so the walls look straight. Step back a little if traffic or passers-by get in the way, and wait a moment for a clear gap. If you go inside, please be thoughtful about photographing other visitors and ask or check the rules for taking pictures indoors before you start.
text.geographic_location: In District Six, a former inner-city residential area of Cape Town, in a former Methodist church building.
text.directions_text: No station or tram stop is listed for this spot. Start from Cape Town city centre and head towards District Six. The museum is in the old church building, and the phone icon on the map is right at the building itself. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) to show the whole church front. Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) only if the pavement is narrow and you cannot step back, and keep the phone level so the walls do not lean.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. Take your photo with the building in front of you.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line up the vertical edges of the church with them. Include a little pavement or street in the foreground so the building feels part of its neighbourhood. For a detail shot, use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) on the doorway or the signage.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the front of the building to focus, then slide the exposure down slightly if the sky is bright so the walls keep their detail.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Daylight, ideally when the front of the building is evenly lit, and a quieter moment to keep the street clear of people and vehicles.

text.access_note: Check the official site before you go for opening arrangements and photography rules.

name: Cape Town Stadium
label: Cape Town Stadium
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Signal Hill' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Signal Hill' (node/287092475): point.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/626140250: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'DHL Stadium' (384 m across).
notes: World Cup stadium set against Signal Hill.

text.description: Cape Town Stadium, known since 2021 as the DHL Stadium for sponsorship reasons, is the largest stadium in the city. It was built for the 2010 FIFA World Cup, and building work began in March 2007 and took 33 months. It was handed over to the City of Cape Town on 14 December 2009. Its capacity was 64,100 for the World Cup and was later reduced to 55,000. It stands in Green Point between Signal Hill and the Atlantic Ocean, close to the city centre and the V&A Waterfront. That position is what makes it photograph so well. From the lookout area on Signal Hill you see the stadium below you against Table Bay, with Table Mountain and the city bowl behind, so one wide frame tells the whole story of the place. Use the default lens (1x) for the full scene, and keep the stadium roughly a third of the way into the picture so the mountain and coastline have room. If you want a closer, cleaner shot of the building, Green Point Park gives a ground-level view of the sweeping mesh roof across open grass. The end of the Breakwater gives a view across the harbour water with the sea air and mist in the frame. The stadium is a secured venue, so take your photos from public land outside the fence. The Signal Hill road can be busy, so pull in only where it is safe and legal.
text.geographic_location: In Green Point, on the Atlantic side of Cape Town's city bowl, between Signal Hill and the sea. It is close to the city centre and the V&A Waterfront, next to Green Point Park.
text.directions_text: On foot, the walk down is roughly 25-30 minutes, though the real route down the hill may differ. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the whole scene of stadium, bay and mountain. Try the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to bring the stadium and the mountain closer together, and the ultra-wide (0.5x) only if the foreground, such as the hillside, adds something, because the stadium will look small.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Signal Hill (lookout area on the hill above Green Point, reached by the Signal Hill road). The stadium sits below the hill against Table Bay, with Table Mountain and the city bowl behind it, shown as a wide aerial-style scene.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and put the stadium on a lower third line, with the mountain filling the upper part and the coastline running across. Keep the horizon level. For an alternative, Green Point Park gives a clean full-building shot of the roof across the open park.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the stadium to set focus and exposure, then slide the exposure down a little so the sky keeps its colour and the mountain does not wash out. Panorama mode can work for the sweep of the bay, if you hold the phone steady and turn slowly.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: The hour before sunset is often said to give the best light. After dusk, use night mode and brace your phone against a wall or railing.

text.access_note: Signal Hill is public land and not a paid viewpoint, but the stadium itself is a secured venue, so shoot from outside the fence and check the official site before you go in case of event closures or photo rules.

photo.artist: Hansueli Krapf This file was uploaded with Commonist.

name: Castle of Good Hope
label: Castle of Good Hope
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Oranje Bastion' (2 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Oranje Bastion' (way/424912998): middle (55 m across); moved 10 m off buildings.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/57263: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Castle of Good Hope' (326 m across).
notes: 17th-century pentagonal fortress, the oldest colonial building in South Africa.

text.description:
The Castle of Good Hope is a star-shaped stone fort with thick yellow walls, and it is a good place to photograph the city's colonial past with Table Mountain behind it. The Dutch East India Company built it between 1666 and 1679, and it is the oldest existing building in South Africa. It once stood on the shore of Table Bay, but land reclamation has left it inland. Its five bastions are named Leerdam, Buuren, Katzenellenbogen, Nassau and Oranje. The yellow paint was originally chosen to reduce the effect of heat and sun. Today it is a provincial heritage site and is described as the best preserved Dutch East India Company fort.

One guide recommends the Oranje Bastion as the best spot for the view, where the fort is in the foreground and Table Mountain and Lion's Head rise behind it. Inside, the outer courtyard gives you the yellow walls and the clock tower, and the De Kat Balcony, rebuilt between 1786 and 1790, has sculptures and a mountain backdrop. The castle's original bell, cast in 1697, is the oldest in South Africa. Weekday visits can start with the Key Ceremony at 10am, when the Castle Guard formally opens the castle. Keep your phone steady against a wall or railing, and watch your footing on the ramparts if it has rained.
text.geographic_location: The castle is in Cape Town, inland from Table Bay on ground that was once shoreline.
text.directions_text: Head from the centre of Cape Town to the castle. If you are near the railway station, keep your phone and any camera gear out of sight between shots. Once inside, follow the signs to the ramparts and the Oranje Bastion. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: For the Oranje Bastion view, start with the default lens (1x) for the fort in the foreground with the mountain behind. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) if you want more of the star-shaped walls and sky. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pull Table Mountain and Lion's Head closer.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject (on top of the bastion, looking toward Table Mountain). The castle in the foreground with Table Mountain and Lion's Head behind it, a clear line of sight over the fortress.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and put the castle roofs and walls in the lower third, with the mountain filling the upper part. If the castle is open, a good alternative is the outer courtyard, where the yellow walls and clock tower frame the shot. Another is the De Kat Balcony, with the 'Kings of the Castle' sculptures in the foreground and the mountain behind.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the mountain to focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly so the sky keeps its colour and the yellow walls do not wash out. Step back from edges and railings when you shoot.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Visit soon after the castle opens, or in the softer light of late afternoon, and check closing times first as they vary. Avoid rainy days if you can, as the ramparts can be slippery.

text.access_note: The viewpoints are inside the castle, which is a ticketed site that may close for film shoots or private events, so check the official site before you go.

name: Lion's Head
label: Lion's Head
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Signal Hill' (2 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Signal Hill' (node/287092475): point.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap node/48944401: the OpenStreetMap point 'Lion's Head'.
notes: Popular peak hike with panoramic views, especially at sunset.

text.description: Lion's Head is the peak that sits between Table Mountain and Signal Hill, and it works as a natural backdrop for almost any Cape Town view. It rises to 669 metres above sea level and is part of Table Mountain National Park. In the 17th century the Dutch called it Leeuwen Kop, and Signal Hill was its 'tail', because the pair look like a crouching lion or a sphinx. That shape is what you are trying to catch in the frame. Signal Hill's broad grassy crest is the easy way to see it. From there Lion's Head rises behind the city bowl, the harbour and the Atlantic seaboard, with the ridge in the foreground. You can reach it by road, so no climbing is needed. The same view is a popular choice for sunset. Keep the mountain's outline clear of the foreground, and let the city and sea fill the lower part of the picture. If you want a different angle, Kloof Corner looks across the gap to Lion's Head with Camps Bay below and suits early light. Bloubergstrand shows it across the bay together with Table Mountain. Parking at Signal Hill is limited and fills quickly around sunset, so arrive early.
text.geographic_location: Lion's Head sits in Cape Town between Table Mountain and Signal Hill, with the city bowl and the Bo-Kaap quarter close by.
text.directions_text: No train stations or tram stops are listed near this spot. Signal Hill can be reached by road, so check a map for the route up. Once you are on the crest, walk to the broad grassy area at the top of the road and look south-west towards Lion's Head. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to take in the city, harbour and sea with the mountain behind. Switch to the default lens (1x) for a calmer, more natural view. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to bring Lion's Head closer and make it look larger against the city.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Signal Hill (broad grassy crest at the top of the road, looking back toward Lion's Head). Lion's Head rising behind the city bowl, harbour and Atlantic seaboard, with the ridge in the foreground.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and place the peak on one of the upper lines, with the city and sea in the lower third. Include a bit of the grassy ridge in the foreground to give depth. If you want a different angle, Kloof Corner shows Lion's Head across the gap with Camps Bay below; take care near its steep edges.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the mountain to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the sky keeps its colour and the peak does not turn into a flat silhouette. Take a few shots as the light changes, and use the telephoto for a tighter version of the same scene.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Around sunset. Arrive early, as parking is limited and fills quickly.

text.access_note: Signal Hill is a free, public viewpoint, but parking is limited; Lion's Head is in Table Mountain National Park, so check the official site before you go if you plan to climb it or fly a drone.

name: Zeitz Museum of Contemporary Art Africa
label: Zeitz MOCAA
camera_source: No separate stand-here point: photographed at the spot itself (indoors, from its top, or right in front of it); drawn as the split pin.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/36852808: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Zeitz Museum of Contemporary Art Africa (MOCAA)' (77 m across).
notes: Contemporary art museum in a converted grain silo with a striking atrium.

text.description: Zeitz MOCAA is a contemporary art museum built inside a 57 m grain silo at the V&A Waterfront. The silo was put up between 1921 and 1924, and the museum opened on 22 September 2017. It is billed as the largest museum of contemporary art from Africa and its diaspora. Heatherwick Studio kept the industrial look of the old concrete structure but carved out its 42 tightly packed cylinders to make galleries and a tall central atrium. The upper floors now have pillowed glass panels, which are the most obvious change from outside. Those bulging windows and the plain concrete make a strong contrast, and that is why the building photographs well. Start with a wide shot of the whole tower, then move in for details of the glass and the concrete. Inside, the atrium has the remaining concrete shafts capped with glass so daylight pours in, giving a 'cathedral-like' feel. The building has nine floors, a sculpture garden on the lower roof, a rooftop restaurant and a coffee shop. The upper part of the tower is The Silo Hotel. Exterior shots are the easy win with a phone. If you go inside, ask staff whether photography is allowed in the galleries and in the atrium, as rules can vary. Keep the phone level, use the gridlines to keep the tall edges straight, and wipe the lens before you start.
text.geographic_location: In the Silo District of the V&A Waterfront. The museum fills the old grain silo building, with The Silo Hotel in its upper floors.
text.directions_text: No station or tram stop is listed for this spot, so head for the V&A Waterfront and then the Silo District, where the tall silo building is easy to spot. Once you are in the Silo District, the phone icon on the map is at the museum itself, so there is no further walk. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) for the full height of the tower and for the atrium if photography is allowed inside. Use the default lens (1x) for general views, and telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for details of the pillowed glass and concrete.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. Move back from the building along the Waterfront paths until the whole tower fits in the frame, and take your wide shots from there.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Switch on the gridlines and line up the vertical edges of the tower with the grid so the building does not lean. Take one full-height shot, then move closer for a diagonal view of the glass panels against the concrete. Inside, if allowed, point the phone upward to catch the glass-topped shafts of the atrium.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the building to set focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the sky is bright, so the concrete keeps its detail and the glass does not wash out. Hold the phone steady and level, as tilting up makes the tower lean.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Soft morning or late-afternoon light usually flatters concrete and glass better than harsh midday sun. Visit when it suits your timings, and check the museum's own site for visiting details.

text.access_note: Check the museum's official site for visiting details. Photograph the exterior from wherever you can see it safely.

name: Signal Hill
label: Signal Hill
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Sea Point promenade' (2 web pages); placed at the stretch of Sea Point promenade nearest the subject (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap node/287092475: the OpenStreetMap point 'Signal Hill'.
notes: Hilltop viewpoint over the city, harbour and Atlantic coast.

text.description: Signal Hill is the flat-topped hill beside Lion's Head and Table Mountain, and from the Sea Point promenade you get the classic low view of it. Lion's Head and Signal Hill together are said to look like a lion sphinx, and from the sea-front the two shapes rise side by side above the coastline. That makes a tidy, layered photo with the sea in the foreground, the buildings of Sea Point in the middle and the hill behind. The promenade is at street level and needs no climb, so it suits a quick stop. The hill has a long working history. Signal flags were once used to send weather warnings and anchoring instructions to ships in the bay, and a time ball was set up here after 1836 so ships could check their clocks. It is still known for the Noon Gun, which fires daily at midday except Sundays. A road runs to the summit, and the guides note the top gets very crowded at sunset with limited parking. The summit is the other good photo spot, with the Noon Gun cannon in the foreground and the city bowl, harbour and Table Mountain behind it. The hill is also one of the only places where the rare Peninsula Shale Renosterveld vegetation survives. Keep the promenade rail or a lamp post out of the corners, and take a few frames with people walking in for scale.
text.geographic_location: Signal Hill sits on the Atlantic side of Cape Town, next to Lion's Head and Table Mountain, overlooking the city centre and the Atlantic Seaboard. The Sea Point promenade is the sea-front walk looking back at it.
text.directions_text: No station or tram stop is listed for this spot, so start from Sea Point and head to the promenade along the sea. For the summit, a road leads up to the top (Signal Hill Road), but check the official site before you go. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Use the default lens (1x) for the whole scene, with sea, hill and Lion's Head together. Switch to telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to bring the hill closer and fill the frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Sea Point promenade. Signal Hill and Lion's Head rising above the Sea Point coastline, shot from street level along the sea.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and put the skyline of the hill on the upper third line, with the sea wall or promenade along the lower third. Try the ultra-wide (0.5x) for a lot of sea and sky, but the hill will look small. If you go up to the summit instead, frame the Noon Gun in the foreground with the city bowl and Table Mountain behind it.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the hill to set focus, then slide the exposure slider down slightly if the sky looks washed out. At 3x or 5x, hold the phone steady against the rail or your body.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Choose a clear day. Go early in the day or later in the afternoon, when the light is softer and the crowds are thinner. If you head up to the summit for sunset, arrive early, as the guides say it fills up and parking is limited.

text.access_note: The promenade is an open public street-side walk; for the summit road, parking and the Noon Gun, check the official site before you go.

name: Greenmarket Square
label: Greenmarket Square
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Old Town House' (1 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Old Town House Museum' (way/609226195): middle (37 m across); moved 10 m off buildings.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/23893904: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Greenmarket Square' (114 m across).
notes: Cobbled square with an African crafts market.

text.description: Greenmarket Square is a historic square in the centre of old Cape Town. It photographs well because old and lively sit side by side: rows of colourful craft stalls in front of historic buildings. The square began with a burgher watch house in 1696. In 1761 that was replaced by the Old Town House, which now holds the Michaelis Collection of art. Over the centuries the square has been a slave market, a vegetable market and a car park. Today it is a flea market selling mainly African souvenirs, crafts and curios. The square and its surrounding buildings were declared a national monument in 1961, and the square was pedestrianised in the early 2000s, so you can stop and frame a shot without worrying about traffic. Near the middle is a hand-operated pump that brings up water from an underground river, a nice small detail for a close-up. A recommended viewpoint for the Old Town House is its facade facing the square, where you can show the 18th-century building with the market stalls in front. Look for its architectural detail and sense of grandeur, and try mid-morning or late afternoon when the light is softer. It is a busy market, so expect people in your frame, and ask before taking close portraits of stallholders.
text.geographic_location: Greenmarket Square is in the city bowl, in the centre of Cape Town, between St George's Mall to the south-east and Long Street to the north-west. Strand Street lies to the north and Wale Street to the south.
text.directions_text: There are no railway or tram stops listed nearby, so go by taxi or ride-hail to the city centre and ask for Greenmarket Square. If you are dropped on Long Street or St George's Mall, walk to the square between Shortmarket Street and Longmarket Street. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the Old Town House with the stalls in front. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if the crowds or the stalls leave you little room to step back. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for architectural details or the hand pump.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand at Old Town House (facade facing the square). The historic 18th-century building as a backdrop to the colourful market stalls.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Switch on gridlines and keep the building's vertical lines straight, with stall colours filling the lower part of the frame. For a different view, try Burg Street, looking along it to the square with the Old Town House on the right of the frame. You could also try the Central Methodist Mission church, which rises above the square beside the Inn on the Square and Tudor Hotels.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the building to set focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the sky is bright so the facade keeps its detail. Ask before using portrait mode on stallholders.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Mid-morning or late afternoon, when the light is not too harsh.

text.access_note: The square is a pedestrianised public market space; if you want to go inside the Old Town House or its art collection, check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: Mid-morning or late afternoon light is gentler on the Old Town House facade than midday light.
The square is likely to be busy with shoppers and tourists while the market is trading.
Entry to the Old Town House and the Michaelis Collection may be ticketed or have set opening times.

name: Long Street
label: Long Street
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Long Street Baths' (2 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Long Street Baths' (way/42353074): middle (87 m across); moved 15 m off buildings.
pin_note: Position from Wikidata Q6673252: kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.
notes: Victorian balconies, bars and bookshops in the city centre.

text.description:
Long Street is one of the best-known streets in Cape Town's City Bowl, and it is easy to see why it draws visitors from all over the world. It is lined with bookshops, restaurants and bars, and it has a lively, slightly bohemian feel. For photographs, the main attraction is its Victorian buildings with wrought-iron balconies, which give the street a strong rhythm of repeating shapes. In the 1970s and 1980s several theatres here staged anti-apartheid plays. Most have since closed and been replaced by restaurants or shops, but the street still has a lot of character.

The best overall view is from the street itself, looking toward the heritage doorway of the Long Street Baths at the top end. Table Mountain shows in the background to one side. Traffic only runs uphill (south-west) here, so cars approach from behind you as you face the baths. Keep to the pavement and watch the traffic.

Once you have the long view, walk along the street and shoot the details: balconies, murals, street signs and people passing. If you want a busier, more varied backdrop, Greenmarket Square is nearby. Street conditions change from day to day, so check what the street is like when you arrive.
text.geographic_location: Long Street runs through the City Bowl, the central part of Cape Town, parallel to Loop Street. The Long Street Baths stand at the top (south-west) end of the street.
text.directions_text: There are no nearby rail stations or tram stops listed, so head for the City Bowl in central Cape Town. The MyCiTi 101 bus runs the length of Long Street, with five stops along it. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the view along the street. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) when you are close to the buildings and want the full height of a balcony. Use 2x-3x telephoto, if your phone has it, to pull Table Mountain closer behind the rooftops.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand at Long Street Baths (in the centre of Long Street, facing the baths' heritage doors). Looking down the street toward the heritage doorway, with Table Mountain visible in the background to one side. Stay on the pavement rather than the roadway.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line the street up with a vertical grid line so the buildings do not lean. Keep the heritage doorway of the baths at the end of the view, with the balconies lining both sides, and let the mountain fill the gap above the rooftops. Afterwards, walk along the street for close-ups of balconies, murals and signs with people passing. Greenmarket Square is a busier alternative nearby.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the sky or the mountain to set focus and exposure, then drag the exposure slider down slightly so the sky keeps its colour and detail. If the street is in shadow, tap a darker building and check the sky has not turned white. In the evening, use night mode and hold the phone still against a wall or post.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Daytime, when the mountain is clear of cloud, gives the best view. Check the sky before you set off.

text.access_note: Long Street is an open public street.
claims_not_in_sources: The Long Street Baths stand at the top (south-west) end of Long Street.
Table Mountain is visible behind the street from the baths, to one side.
Keeping to the pavement is safer than standing in the roadway.
Table Mountain can be hidden by cloud, so the view is best on a clear day.
Greenmarket Square is near Long Street.

name: Cape Town City Hall
label: City Hall
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Grand Parade' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Grand Parade' (way/5216621): middle (267 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/1524822758: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Cape Town City Hall' (133 m across).
notes: Edwardian building where Mandela addressed crowds after his release.

text.description: Cape Town City Hall is a large Edwardian building finished in 1905, built from honey-coloured limestone brought from Bath in England. It sits on the Grand Parade, just west of the Castle, and its clock tower gives the front a clear, easy-to-recognise shape. The tower clock chimes the Westminster quarters, so you may hear it while you shoot. The building also has a place in recent history: on 11 February 1990, hours after his release from prison, Nelson Mandela made his first public speech from its balcony. A bronze statue of him now looks out over the Grand Parade. Check on the day exactly where the statue stands (balcony or front steps) before you plan a shot around it. The best view is from the open square of the Grand Parade, facing the front facade across from Darling Street. From there the whole facade and clock tower fit in one frame, and Table Mountain can rise above the roofline when the air is clear. Early morning is the best time to go, as the eastern facade is fully lit and the wind is calmer. On peak summer afternoons the south-east wind, known as the Cape Doctor, can blow hard across the square. Keep your phone upright and level so the tower does not lean.
text.geographic_location: In Cape Town's city centre, on the Grand Parade, to the west of the Castle. The City Hall faces the open square across from Darling Street.
text.directions_text: No station or tram stop is listed for this spot, so simply head for the Grand Parade in the city centre. From there the City Hall is to the south-west, about 2 minutes on foot. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit the full facade and clock tower in one frame. Switch to the default lens (1x) for a more natural look with less edge stretching. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out the clock tower, or the Mandela statue, from the square.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Grand Parade (open square facing the City Hall's front facade, across from Darling Street). The full Edwardian facade and clock tower of the City Hall, with Table Mountain rising above the roofline behind it when conditions are clear. The statue of Nelson Mandela is another good subject, with the building's architecture behind it.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line the tower up with a vertical line so it stands straight. Leave some sky above the tower so Table Mountain can show behind it. For a second picture, zoom in on the Mandela statue with the facade behind it.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the pale stone of the facade to focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the sky and the limestone keep their detail. If the lights are on for an event after dark, try night mode and hold the phone steady against something solid.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning, when the eastern facade is fully lit and the wind is calmer. Late afternoon on peak summer days can be windy across the square.

text.access_note: The Grand Parade is an open square, but Cape Town Tourism says you can ask the security guard for permission to step inside for photos, and interior access depends on events, so check the official site before you go.

name: Green Point Lighthouse
label: Green Point Lighthouse
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Green Point Park' (1 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Green Point Park' (way/44948367): edge nearest the subject (789 m across).
pin_note: Position from OSM W134572381 (Green Point Lighthouse): kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.
notes: Red-and-white striped lighthouse, the oldest in South Africa.

text.description:
Green Point Lighthouse is a red-and-white lighthouse in Cape Town's Green Point area. It makes a tidy, graphic photo because the stripes stand out against the modern apartment blocks around it and the slopes of Signal Hill behind. The lighthouse is a short walk to the north-west, so you can see it before you reach it.

Keep the picture simple. Put the lighthouse slightly off-centre, leave some sky above it, and let Signal Hill fill the background. Turn on your phone's gridlines and line the tower up with a vertical line so it stands straight. If you walk on to the lighthouse itself, a different view opens up: the tower fills the frame, with the Waterfront promenade stretching out behind you. Any visit inside the lighthouse may be ticketed or have restricted days and hours, so check the official site before you go. The outside views need no ticket to photograph from the park.
text.geographic_location: The lighthouse is in Green Point, Cape Town, close to the Waterfront promenade. The park view looks towards it with Signal Hill rising behind.
text.directions_text: The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Use the default lens (1x) for the main shot. It shows the lighthouse, the apartment blocks and Signal Hill together. Pinch to 2x if you want the tower larger without moving. Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) only if you walk up close and want the whole tower in the frame, and keep the phone level so the sides don't lean.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Green Point Park. The red-and-white lighthouse framed by modern apartment blocks, with the slopes of Signal Hill rising behind it. The lighthouse is to the north-west.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Use the open lawn as foreground and keep the lighthouse a little off-centre with Signal Hill behind it. Line the tower up with a vertical gridline. As an alternative, walk to the lighthouse and shoot with the Waterfront promenade stretching out behind you.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Switch on gridlines. Tap the lighthouse to focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little if the white parts of the tower look washed out against the sky.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Morning light suits the clean, architectural shot. Late afternoon is also recommended, so try whichever fits your day.

text.access_note: The park view is from a public park; for the lighthouse itself, including any tour or climb, check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: Green Point Park is an open public park that can be entered freely.
Morning light suits the architectural shot of the lighthouse, and late afternoon is also a good time (research sources differ).
The lighthouse is close to the Waterfront promenade.
Dragging the exposure slider down can help keep white surfaces from washing out against a bright sky.

name: Company's Garden
label: Company's Garden
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Rose Garden' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'The Rose Garden' (way/233192312): middle (90 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/8035472: 'Artillerymen's Memorial', the best-known feature inside 'Company's Garden' (577 m across).
notes: Historic public garden in the city centre.

text.description:
Company's Garden is a large public park in the middle of Cape Town, and the oldest garden in South Africa. Dutch East India Company settlers began it in the 1650s to grow fresh vegetables for the settlement and for ships rounding the Cape. Master gardener Hendrik Boom prepared the first ground for sowing on 29 April 1652. Today it is a shady place of lawns, benches, an avenue of old trees, a fish pond and historic statues. It is also a national heritage site.

The best photo here is in the Rose Garden, which was designed and built in 1929. Guides often describe it as a favourite photo spot. You get rose beds in the foreground and, often, Table Mountain behind them, so one frame shows both the garden and the city's famous backdrop. The beds bloom in spring and summer, so they may look sparser in winter.

For a second picture, walk to Government Avenue, the oak-lined path through the garden. Stand at one end and shoot down its length so the branches frame the path. Squirrels, doves and Egyptian geese are among the animals found in the park, and they make good small subjects if you are patient. If you photograph people up close, ask first.
text.geographic_location: Company's Garden sits in the Cape Town city centre, next to Parliament and Tuynhuys. The Iziko South African Museum and Iziko National Gallery are inside the grounds.
text.directions_text: From the city centre, head to the garden. The Rose Garden is the recommended viewpoint in the garden. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the rose beds with the mountain behind. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit more roses into the foreground. Try telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to bring Table Mountain closer.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Rose Garden. Rose beds in the foreground, with Table Mountain often visible in the background of the frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and place the horizon on the upper line, so the roses fill the lower part of the frame and the mountain sits above them. Crouch a little to make the flowers larger against the skyline. For a different shot, walk to Government Avenue and shoot straight down the oak-lined path so the trees frame it.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the mountain to set focus, then slide the exposure down slightly so the sky keeps its detail. If you want the flowers sharp as well, tap a nearby rose and check how the sky looks. Try portrait mode for a single bloom.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon, when the light is softer. Midday sun is harsh. Roses are at their best in spring and summer.

text.access_note: Open public garden that is free to walk through; personal photography is generally fine, but professional shoots and drone use may need City of Cape Town permits, so check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: Company's Garden is in the Gardens area of Cape Town.
Government Avenue is oak-lined and can be photographed down its length.
Slightly lowering the exposure on a phone helps keep sky detail when the mountain is in the frame.

name: Parliament of South Africa
label: Parliament
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Government Avenue' (3 web pages); placed at the stretch of Government Avenue nearest the subject (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from Wikidata Q2185780: kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.
notes: Seat of the national legislature next to the Company's Garden.

text.description:
This is where South Africa's lawmakers meet. Cape Town is the country's legislative capital, while the government sits in Pretoria, a split that goes back to the foundation of the Union. The Houses of Parliament were built between 1875 and 1884. A fire in early January 2022 destroyed the National Assembly's session room, and the rebuild has a target completion date of June 2027. So the building you see may look a little different from older photos.

From here you look at the building's rear, garden-side façade. Its evenly spaced columns are easy to pick out, and the avenue's trees make a natural frame down both sides of the shot. It is a calm, orderly picture: straight lines, repeating columns and green leaves, with the building a short step ahead of you.

For a front view, the street side has a central portico with paired columns. It is worth a look if you have time, but the avenue is the easier place to take your time and get a clean frame. Exterior photos are generally fine. Keep your phone away from the entrances and security staff, and follow any signs. Inside the building, photography is restricted.
text.geographic_location: In central Cape Town, at the edge of the Company's Garden.
text.directions_text: From there the Parliament building is to the south-east, about 1 minute on foot. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for a natural view of the façade framed by trees. If the whole width does not fit, switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x). Use the telephoto (2x or more) for a tighter shot of the columns.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Government Avenue (rear (garden-side) façade, looking across the avenue). The building's rear façade with its evenly spaced columns, framed by the tree-lined avenue and the Company's Garden. The Parliament building is ahead of you to the south-east.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on your gridlines and line up the columns with the vertical grid lines so the building does not lean. Keep a tree trunk or an overhanging branch on each side to frame the shot. For a different view, try the Company's Garden for lawns and trees in the foreground, or the street on the front side (often given as Parliament Street; check the street name on the map) for the front façade with its central portico and paired columns.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the building to focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the sky is bright, so the stonework keeps its detail. Take a few frames with different people on the avenue and pick the tidiest.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light and gentler shadows between the columns. Check the light on the day, as the trees can throw patchy shade across the façade.

text.access_note: The exterior can generally be photographed from the public avenue and streets, but interior and chamber photography is restricted, so follow signs and security staff and check the official site before you go.

name: St. George's Cathedral
label: St George's Cathedral
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Wale Street' (2 web pages); placed at the stretch of Wale Street nearest the subject (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/141281671: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'St. George's Cathedral' (82 m across).
notes: Anglican cathedral associated with Desmond Tutu.

text.description: St George's Cathedral is the Anglican cathedral of Cape Town and the seat of the Archbishop of Cape Town. Sir Herbert Baker designed it, and the foundation stones were laid in 1901. The north transept was finished in 1936, which completed his design. It photographs well because the Neo-Gothic front and spires can be seen straight on from across the road, with the stonework filling the frame. The bell tower is clad in Table Mountain Sandstone, which gives the building a warm, solid look in pictures. The cathedral is also known for its part in the struggle against apartheid. Desmond Tutu led marches and campaigns from its front steps, and it became known as the "people's cathedral". It was declared a provincial heritage site in 2014. Take one wide shot to show the whole facade and spires, then move in closer for details such as the entrance and the stonework. For a greener, more framed view, Company's Gardens, just beside the cathedral, shows it through the trees. Be aware of traffic and other people on the pavement, and keep clear of the entrance so you don't block anyone.
text.geographic_location: St George's Cathedral stands in central Cape Town, at the corner of Wale Street and Government Avenue, at the lower end of the Company's Gardens.
text.directions_text: No Underground, train or tram stop is listed for this spot, so walk to Wale Street from the city centre or from Company's Gardens. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) if you are close to the building, because it fits the full facade and both spires in one frame. Switch to the default lens (1x) for a more natural look with less stretching at the edges. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the spires, windows and carved stonework.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Wale Street (directly opposite the cathedral's front, on the pavement facing the west front). The full Neo-Gothic facade and spires of the cathedral, framed straight on from across the road.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and line up the central axis of the building with the middle vertical line, so the facade looks balanced and the towers stay upright. Keep the phone level and don't tilt it upwards, or the spires will lean inwards. Leave a little sky above the spires. For a different view, Company's Gardens gives a softer picture of the cathedral seen through the trees.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the stonework to set focus, then use the exposure slider to bring the brightness down slightly if the sky is bright, so the facade keeps its detail. If people are in the way, take a Live Photo or a few quick shots and pick the one with the clearest view.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Soft light early or later in the day usually suits the stonework better than harsh midday sun, and the pavement tends to be quieter early on.

text.access_note: The cathedral is a working place of worship, so photography may not be welcome during services or private events; check the official site before you go if you plan to go inside.
claims_not_in_sources: Photography from the pavement of Wale Street is generally allowed, but not during services or private events.
